title: Ronald Fisher and the Popularizing of the p-value (1925)
explainer: The p-value traces back to Karl Pearson's chi-squared work around 1900, but it was Ronald Fisher's 1925 book Statistical Methods for Research Workers that popularized it as a research tool and proposed p = 0.05 as a conventional significance threshold. Every ML paper that reports a result as 'statistically significant,' runs a t-test on benchmark scores, or argues a new method beats a baseline is leaning on a 100-year-old convention that was never meant to be a universal bar for truth - knowing its origin as a practical heuristic, not a law of nature, is exactly the kind of skepticism research literacy requires when reading a claim.

title: The 2015 Reproducibility Project and the Replication Crisis
explainer: In 2015, the Open Science Collaboration, coordinated by psychologist Brian Nosek, attempted to redo 97 psychology studies that had reported significant effects; only about a third replicated successfully, and the effects that did replicate were on average roughly half the size originally claimed. The same skepticism now applies squarely to ML research, where benchmark leaderboard gains, ablation claims, and 'emergent' capabilities are frequently found not to hold up under independent re-implementation - research literacy means treating a single paper's reported result the way a careful reader treats a single un-replicated psychology finding.
